## German Shepherd Dog ranks No. 4 among the most registered breeds
Credit: Steve Smith / Unsplash
The German Shepherd Dog holds No. 4 on the AKC's most popular breeds list, a rank it has kept for four straight years of registration data. The breed has not fallen out of the top five in more than a decade, and it sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s.
Germany produced the breed in the late 1800s, largely through the standardizing work of Max von Stephanitz, who wanted a herding dog evaluated on working ability rather than looks. That priority carried over to other jobs. Police departments, militaries, and detection programs adopted the breed early, and it remains one of the dogs most often used for scent work, patrol work, and search and rescue in the U.S.
Males generally stand 24 to 26 inches at the shoulder and females 22 to 24 inches, with weight usually falling between 50 and 90 pounds. A dense double coat is standard, most often in black and tan, though sable, solid black, and other patterns are recognized. Shedding runs year-round and spikes during seasonal coat changes, which makes brushing several times a week routine.
Owners describe the temperament in similar terms: alert, fast to learn, and closely attached to a handler, often bonding hardest with one or two people in the household. That focus makes the breed responsive in training and also means it needs an outlet. A German Shepherd left in a yard without structured exercise or obedience work commonly develops barking, digging, or separation anxiety.
Health screening carries real weight with this breed. Hip and elbow dysplasia are both documented, and the exaggerated rear angulation seen in some show lines remains a point of dispute among breeders on orthopedic grounds. Degenerative myelopathy, a progressive spinal cord disease that produces hind-limb weakness, appears in German Shepherds more often than in most breeds, and a DNA test for the associated risk variant is available. The breed is also prone to bloat, which requires emergency veterinary care. Hip, elbow, and genetic screening results on both parents are reasonable things to request from a breeder.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

### According to the American Kennel Club the Top Ten List of Dogs for 2013 are:
1.   Labrador Retrievers (Sporting Group)  
2.   German Shepherds (Herding Group)  
3.   Golden Retrievers (Sporting Group)  
4.   Beagles (Hound Group)

5.   Bulldogs (Non-Sporting Group)  
6.   Yorkshire Terriers (Toy Group)  
7.   Boxers (Working Group)  
8.   Poodles (Non-Sporting Group)  
9.   Rottweilers (Working Group)  
10.   Dachshunds (Hound Group)
While the Labrador Retriever has been in the number one slot for several years the Rottweiler has made a significant rise up the “Most Wanted” list because back in 2003 and 2008 they were only ranked in 15th and 14th place, respectively. My favorite, Great Danes ranked#16…not too bad.  If you want to see where your dog ranks you can check out the AKC’s listwhich is based on dog registrations.
This is Cece the Chocolate Lab – Just look at that face….no wonder Labs are the #1 dog.
Labrador Retriever – the #1 AKC registered dog!

The German Shepherd Dog holds No. 4 on the AKC's most popular breeds list, a rank it has kept for four straight years of registration data. The breed has not fallen out of the top five in more than a decade, and it sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s.
Germany produced the breed in the late 1800s, largely through the standardizing work of Max von Stephanitz, who wanted a herding dog evaluated on working ability rather than looks. That priority carried over to other jobs. Police departments, militaries, and detection programs adopted the breed early, and it remains one of the dogs most often used for scent work, patrol work, and search and rescue in the U.S.
Males generally stand 24 to 26 inches at the shoulder and females 22 to 24 inches, with weight usually falling between 50 and 90 pounds. A dense double coat is standard, most often in black and tan, though sable, solid black, and other patterns are recognized. Shedding runs year-round and spikes during seasonal coat changes, which makes brushing several times a week routine.
Owners describe the temperament in similar terms: alert, fast to learn, and closely attached to a handler, often bonding hardest with one or two people in the household. That focus makes the breed responsive in training and also means it needs an outlet. A German Shepherd left in a yard without structured exercise or obedience work commonly develops barking, digging, or separation anxiety.
Health screening carries real weight with this breed. Hip and elbow dysplasia are both documented, and the exaggerated rear angulation seen in some show lines remains a point of dispute among breeders on orthopedic grounds. Degenerative myelopathy, a progressive spinal cord disease that produces hind-limb weakness, appears in German Shepherds more often than in most breeds, and a DNA test for the associated risk variant is available. The breed is also prone to bloat, which requires emergency veterinary care. Hip, elbow, and genetic screening results on both parents are reasonable things to request from a breeder.

Credit: Canva Images

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash

Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.

Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## How the French Bulldog overtook a three-decade champion

The Labrador first reached No. 1 in 1991 and stayed there through 2021. Its hold rested on range. The same dog worked as a hunting retriever, a guide dog and a suburban family pet, and it fit easily into houses with yards and open space nearby. Those conditions described much of American suburban growth through the 1990s and 2000s.

A 70-pound sporting dog does not. Small-space living has become a larger part of the American housing picture than it was when the Labrador's streak began.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.

## How does the AKC actually decide which breeds are 'most popular'?
The American Kennel Club compiles its annual breed popularity ranking from litter and individual dog registrations submitted by owners and breeders across its recognized breed list, which now includes 201 breeds as of the AKC's most recent count (American Kennel Club, 2024). A breed's rank reflects how many dogs of that breed were registered that calendar year, not how many actually live in U.S. households, since mixed-breed dogs and unregistered purebreds never appear in the count at all. This means popular family breeds with casual owners who skip registration can be undercounted relative to breeds favored by competitive breeders and exhibitors who register consistently.
Because the list only reflects AKC-registered purebreds, it also excludes the millions of dogs adopted from shelters and rescues each year. The ASPCA estimates that roughly 3.1 million dogs enter U.S. animal shelters annually, and a large share of those are mixed breed or unknown parentage (ASPCA, n.d.). So the AKC ranking is best read as a snapshot of purebred registration trends, useful for spotting rising and falling trends, rather than a full census of every dog breed living in the country.

## Quick decision guide


## Which breeds have actually topped the U.S. popularity charts recently?
The French Bulldog held the number one spot on the AKC's registration list, a dramatic rise for a breed that ranked outside the top 50 as recently as 2010 (American Kennel Club, 2024). Labrador Retrievers, the AKC's most registered breed for 31 consecutive years before being overtaken, still sit firmly in the top five, alongside Golden Retrievers, German Shepherd Dogs, and Poodles in their various sizes. Bulldogs, Rottweilers, and Dachshunds round out much of the remaining top ten in recent years.
This lineup reflects a mix of longstanding family favorites and breeds boosted by social media visibility and celebrity ownership, both of which the AKC itself has cited as drivers behind the French Bulldog's climb. Owners searching for a breed based purely on popularity rank should remember that a dog's suitability for their specific household, activity level, and living space matters far more than where it lands on a national chart.

## What are the AKC's seven breed groups, and why do they matter?
The AKC sorts its recognized breeds into seven groups — Sporting, Hound, Working, Terrier, Toy, Non-Sporting, and Herding — based largely on the original job a breed was developed to perform (American Kennel Club, n.d.). Sporting breeds like Labrador and Golden Retrievers were bred to flush and retrieve game, Herding breeds like German Shepherds and Border Collies were bred to move livestock, and Working breeds such as Rottweilers and Boxers were developed for guarding, pulling, or rescue tasks.
Knowing a dog's group is a genuinely useful shortcut for predicting temperament and exercise needs before ever meeting the breed. Herding and Sporting dogs generally need substantial daily physical and mental work or they develop destructive habits, while Toy group breeds are bred primarily as companions and typically tolerate smaller living spaces better. The Non-Sporting group is essentially a catch-all for breeds, like the Bulldog and Dalmatian, that don't fit neatly into the other six categories.
